By late afternoon, the couple returned to the waterfront penthouse. The golden light of the late-October sun poured through the wide glass windows of the master suite, casting long, elegant shadows across the hardwood floors.

Clara walked over to the grand piano in the corner of the living room, her fingers resting lightly on the ivory keys without pressing them down, listening to the ambient hum of the city below. The harbor traffic moved with a steady, unhurried grace; the distant sound of a ferry horn echoed across the water like a peaceful lullaby.

Julian walked in carrying two crystal glasses of sparkling cider, handing one to her before leaning against the polished wood of the instrument. "The architect called about the weekend house in Maine," he mentioned casually. "The foundation repairs are finished, and the security upgrades—the non-tactical kind, just standard storm shutters and modern locks—are fully installed."

Clara looked up, her expression brightening. "Are we actually going to spend a weekend somewhere without checking the perimeter locks every two hours?"

"That is the official itinerary, Counselor," Julian smiled, clinking his glass against hers. "A weekend of doing absolutely nothing productive, reading paper books by a stone fireplace, and complaining about the weather."

"I accept those terms," she murmured, taking a sip of the crisp cider.

The weight of their extraordinary history hung in the room like a badge of honor, but it no longer defined their future. Their story was no longer written in code names, offshore wire transfers, and midnight flights across international borders. It was written in the quiet safety of the Boston waterfront, in the steady rhythm of their shared heartbeat, and in the unwritten canvas of a tomorrow that belonged entirely to them.
